Diseases of the Hematological System  567
Sideroblastic anemia, another disorder resulting from abnor-
mal heme synthesis, actually presents clinically as iron overload 
due to adjustments for poor oxygenation. Iron absorption and 
RBC production are increased to compensate for ineﬀ ective
oxygen transport.22 Th ere are presently eight characterized 
forms of sideroblastic anemia identiﬁ ed by the genetic muta-
tion that is present, and all have characteristic mitochondrial 
iron overloading.23
Th e rate of hemoglobin synthesis is also a factor in blood
disorders. Iron availability dictates the rate of heme synthesis.
If there is low iron intake or absorption, there will be little 
hemoglobin available. Alternatively, if there is low folate or 
cyanocobalamin, rapidly dividing and diﬀ erentiating cells like 
the RBC are aﬀ ected, and there will be adequate or excessive
hemoglobin inserted into fewer RBC. As the circulating RBC
die oﬀ  without adequate replacement, the oxygen tension falls 
and erythropoietin is produced in greater quantities by the kid-
ney. Homeostatic mechanisms eventually fail to compensate, 
resulting in anemia.5, 24
As the RBC age and die, they are engulfed by macrophages
and the hemoglobin is recycled. Th e proteins are hydrolyzed 
into their component amino acids, and those amino acids are 
picked up from the liver for reutilization. Iron is also recycled 
and either stored in the liver complexed to ferritin or utilized.
